>The name
>Why the process matters
Oxygen is a benchmark for learning from real-world human–agent projects.
Real projects. Reviewed lessons. Evidence you can check.
Real projects, real workflows
Real projects, in sequence
Oxygen includes long-horizon, complex work traces recorded from the first meeting to the final outcome.
Follow the attempts, feedback, and decisions behind a project. See how one step changed the next and what the recorded outcome supports.
Human experience, not just agent traces
Human judgment, preserved
Oxygen traces include meetings that capture decisions, and human–agent sessions that capture execution, correction, and iteration.
You know which correction changed the direction and why an approach was abandoned. Your review turns recorded activity into credible research material.
Safe, scalable collection
Lessons you can take with you
Oxygen uses automated tools to filter high-value traces locally and remove sensitive information before anything is shared.
Get a readable summary and reusable skill candidates, linked to evidence. Correct the wording, keep useful lessons, and export files for future work.
Evaluation: whether experience changes behavior
A benchmark you can shape
Oxygen uses human-authored lessons to test whether project experience changes what an agent does next.
Help establish which lessons matter. Current scoring compares extracted lessons with reviewed references; the next goal is to test their use on new tasks.
How we turn a project into an open dataset
How to start with your project

You point Oxygen to the project.
Local agents prepare the data. You approve the final release.

Choose a project you know.
Review the lessons. Export what you want to keep.
Point Oxygen to a repository, Claude or Codex histories, agent memory, exported chats, meeting notes, transcripts, or recordings.
Open the Contributor Devkit in a project with recorded Codex or Claude Code sessions. Follow its quick start to prepare a run.
We find the conversations, meetings, memories, and files related to the project.
Gather the supported session records associated with your project. Other project records can provide additional context.
We summarize the records and organize the important events into a chronological project timeline.
Read a summary of the important attempts, corrections, and decisions, with the order and recorded outcomes preserved.
We mask low-level tool traces and remove credentials, personal identifiers, private infrastructure, and other sensitive information.
Prepare a redacted version, then check it for sensitive details yourself. Automated redaction can miss information.
We surface uncertain or high-signal moments, show every proposed change as a diff, and let you delete, rewrite, or keep the content.
Check the summary and supporting evidence. Accept, edit, or decline each skill candidate, and add important context the system missed.
We package only the data you approve into a sanitized, contribution-ready project dataset.
Export your reviewed files for your own use. Contact the Oxygen team to discuss including your project in the dataset.
Nothing is uploaded until you review and approve the final export.
Review files before sharing. Preparation uses model workers on your chosen host; check its data handling before processing private records.
How are agents evaluated on Oxygen datasets
What did the agent learn—and can it use it?
Read the project. Write down what you learned.
Learn from a project. Test what carries forward.
A learning method sees the complete project trajectory.
Each method reads the project history, including feedback and decisions.
It never sees the human-authored ground truth.
It does not see the contributor-reviewed reference lessons.
We compare what it learned with the lessons written by the people who completed the project.
Current scoring compares extracted lessons with those references. Our next goal is skill-level evaluation on new tasks, including methods learned through a sequence of corrections.

The method learns the complete project trajectory.
The method processes the project records in its own way.
The learning process is flexible, while the final outcome is constrained to be a verifiable checklist: what they learned, when it takes account.
It reports reusable lessons and when they apply. This makes different learning approaches easier to compare.
One fixed prompt asks every method to list what should persist from the project.
A shared prompt asks each method to report what it learned.
Whatever the method produces: a memory store, a skill file, or another representation, we convert it into the same final format.
Memories, skills, and other representations are expressed in a common format for evaluation.
We compare the extracted lessons with the human-authored ground truth.
We compare reported lessons with the reviewed references.
Results are reported with precision, recall, F1, and a no-context control.
Precision, recall, and F1 measure reference matching. A baseline without project history helps show what the model already knows.
